::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The short version
- **Finish line:** you can say who governs REDS, how the 2026 contract round is built, what "REDS V"
  does and doesn't mean in the records, and what a contributing blood center signs up for.
- **Punchline:** a regional hub has invited Lakeshore to contribute. The Director's decision on
  RSH-0107 is **yes in principle, with conditions**, and the first condition is that no BECS record
  or workflow changes.
- **The rule in one line:** REDS findings are research evidence, not regulation. Your obligations
  come from the contract chain, human-subjects rules and HIPAA, and FDA rules on the BECS records
  you read from, each in its own tier.
- **Monday question:** "Which contract is our hub funded under, and what exactly does our
  agreement with the hub say we deliver, how often, and in what format?"
- **The trap:** treating the invitation as an IT project. It is a governance decision first. The
  extract is the easy part.
:::

## The invitation

The email from the hub's program office is polite and specific. One of the REDS program's regional
hubs is looking for contributing blood centers in the current contract round. It would want
recurring donor, donation and component extracts from Lakeshore's BECS (Blood Establishment
Computer Software), linked into the program's database, plus occasional rapid-response studies
that use retained donation samples.

The medical director forwards it within the hour: "This is exactly the research we should be part
of. I'll be the scientific lead on our side." Then the CIO replies-all: "Great. What does this cost
us in IT, and what are we signing up for?" Regulatory affairs adds: "Is any of this FDA-regulated?"
Your Quality Analyst comes to your desk with a narrower question: "Do research extracts touch our
BECS records?"

You open Lakeshore's internal research participation file, **RSH-0107**, and write four questions
at the top. Who is actually asking us, and who governs them? What contract sits behind the request?
Which rules reach us? What would we commit to? This lesson answers those four, then ends with the
decision you record in the file.

## What REDS is, and where it came from

REDS stands for the Recipient Epidemiology and Donor Evaluation Study, a research program funded by
NHLBI (the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, part of NIH, the National Institutes of
Health). The 2022 program-design paper (Josephson et al., *Transfusion*) describes the lineage in
its introduction (read on PubMed Central; our local excerpt file holds other sections). In the paper's words, the programs "evolved from the Retrovirus Epidemiology
Donor Study (REDS), 1989–2001 and REDS-II, 2004–2012." The local excerpts of the paper also say the
current phase, REDS-IV-P (Pediatric), was "launched in 2019 by NHLBI in collaboration with National
Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD)." Our earlier project notes add REDS-III
between REDS-II and REDS-IV-P, and the paper's own references to REDS-III data (see below) fit that.
The paper's years for REDS-III were not checked, so this course does not state them.

The shift worth noticing is what the data looks like. Early work centered on blood availability and
infectious risk. The paper describes today's programs as epidemiological research on "the entire
transfusion chain, from donors to recipients." The paper calls the technical backbone the
**V2V (vein-to-vein) database**: donor and donation information, the manufactured components, and
hospital patient data, linked so that "blood products can be tracked from donation to
transfusion." Module 2 takes that database apart. Here you only need to know why a blood center's
BECS data is valuable to it: the donor-to-component half of the chain only exists in blood-center
systems.

### What "REDS V" means, and doesn't

People, including people in this curriculum's audience, call the current round "REDS V." Say this
plainly once: **the official records still describe REDS-IV-P phase 3, and none of them use the name
"REDS-V."** The 2026 contract abstracts in NIH RePORTER (the public database of NIH awards) still
call the program REDS-IV-P and describe each contract as being "for phase 3." This course follows
the records. It will not assert a "REDS-V" name, structure or requirement. If a hub's materials use
that name, treat it as their shorthand and ask which contract and protocol the invitation actually
rests on. Re-check NHLBI's REDS page before you rely on any later phase name.

## Why this governance matters to a Director

Every failure mode in research participation starts with someone saying yes to "a study" without
asking who the study answers to. A data feed gets built for a request that never went through the
right approval. Or two people at Lakeshore each promise something different to different parties.
Or a research extract quietly becomes a second, unofficial copy of BECS data with no owner.

The ITSM bridge is **service level management and supplier management, with a funder in the
background**. You would never accept a new recurring integration without knowing who the
customer is, what the agreement says, who can change the requirements, and who is on the hook when
it breaks. REDS participation is that, plus a layer you don't normally have: the "customer"
is a federally funded research program with its own oversight bodies, and the data concerns people
who never signed up for IT operations.

## The rule in plain English

Four things are true at once, and each belongs to a different tier:

1. **REDS is research, not regulation.** Its papers and findings can inform policy. They bind no one.
   This is the same "research evidence" tier the
   [regulatory landscape orientation](../../../foundations/regulatory-landscape-orientation/index.qmd)
   keeps separate from statute, FDA regulation, FDA guidance and AABB Standards.
2. **Participation is arranged through contracts and agreements.** NHLBI funds the program through
   contracts to organizations; a contributing blood center's commitments come from its agreement
   with the hub, not from a regulation about REDS.
3. **Separate rules reach the data itself.** Human-subjects rules (the Common Rule), HIPAA, and NIH
   policies on data management and security apply to the *data*, whatever tier REDS sits in.
   Modules 3 to 5 cover them.
4. **FDA rules still govern the BECS records you read from.** A research extract does not change
   what those records are or how you protect them. See
   [BECS in the pipeline](../../blood-center-operations/becs-in-the-pipeline/index.qmd).

## Who governs REDS today

The paper's Section 2 lists the bodies that shape the program. Quote first, then the caution about
how far we can interpret it:

> The NHLBI, NICHD, REDS-IV-P Executive Committee, US and Brazil Steering Committees, Observational
> Study Monitoring Board, External Review Panel, and REDS-IV-P committees (e.g.,
> Maternal/In-utero/Neonatal/Kids [MINeKids], Publications, and Mentoring committees) all help
> either to guide or monitor the studies and activities of REDS-IV-P.

*(Josephson et al., Transfusion 2022, Section 2, from `sources/nih/reds-iv-p-program-design-2022.md`.)*

**The paper lists these bodies and says they "guide or monitor." It does not describe each one's
authority, membership or procedures in the excerpts this course holds.** The table below gives each
body's role only as far as the paper or the plain generic meaning of the name supports. Where the
paper is silent, the table says so. Don't present the "generic" column as REDS fact.

| Body | What the paper says | Plain generic meaning of the name | What we don't know from the paper |
|---|---|---|---|
| **NHLBI** | Launched REDS-IV-P in 2019 | The NIH institute that funds the program | Its contracting officers' day-to-day role |
| **NICHD** | Launched it "in collaboration with" NHLBI | The NIH institute focused on child health, which fits the pediatric emphasis | How the collaboration works |
| **Executive Committee** | Named as one of the guiding or monitoring bodies | Typically the program's top operating group | Membership, decision rights |
| **US and Brazil Steering Committees** | Named; two committees, one per country program | Typically coordinate the studies of each national program | Who sits on them, what they approve |
| **Observational Study Monitoring Board** | Named | An independent body that reviews how observational studies are running | Its charter, what it can halt |
| **External Review Panel** | Named | Outside reviewers of the program's work | Scope, frequency |
| **Program committees** | Examples: MINeKids, Publications, Mentoring | Working groups for topics, papers and trainee support | The full list today |

For you, the practical reading is this. **Operational questions about data deliverables go through
your hub, and the hub's contract points back to NHLBI.** The committees are why a study's design,
publication and data use are not up to any single blood center. You will not negotiate with them.
You will be bound by what they decide, through the hub's agreement and study protocols.

### The people who actually do the work

The paper also describes the working structure. The US program comprises "4 hubs," each including
blood centers and several participating hospitals, plus a **Center for Transfusion Laboratory
Studies (CTLS)** and a **Data Coordinating Center (DCC)**. In plain terms:

- **Hubs** are the regional groupings of blood centers and hospitals that do the data collection
  and studies. A contributing blood center like Lakeshore would join through one.
- **The DCC** receives, validates and manages the data. The paper says donor, donation, component
  and patient data are "extracted and transferred to the DCC's Amazon Web Services Virtual Private
  Cloud using secure data transfer (sFTP) keys," with submissions tracked on dashboards. That's the
  paper describing the program's own architecture. Lakeshore's systems are its own business, and
  this lesson does not name any.
- **The CTLS** does laboratory studies, which is where retained samples fit.

## How the 2026 contract round is structured

NIH RePORTER (retrieved 2026-11-13 into `sources/nih/reds-2026-contracts.md`) lists federal award
records. These are facts about who holds which contract. They are not guidance and say nothing about
who a given blood center partners with. Lakeshore is not tied to any organization named here.

| Contract role | Holder, per RePORTER | Period as listed |
|---|---|---|
| Regional hub | Columbia University Health Sciences | 2026-09-30 to 2027-09-29 |
| Regional hub | Emory University | 2026-09-30 to 2027-09-29 |
| Regional hub | Versiti Blood Health, Inc. | 2026-09-30 to 2027-09-29 |
| Regional hub | Vitalant | 2026-09-30 to 2027-09-29 |
| Data Coordinating Center | Westat, Inc. | 2026-09-30 to 2033-09-29 |
| Center for Transfusion Laboratory Studies | Columbia University Health Sciences | 2026-09-30 to 2027-09-29 |
| REDS Brazil | Vitalant | 2026-09-30 to 2033-09-29 |

Read that carefully:

- **Seven contract records, four kinds of work.** Four hub contracts, one DCC, one CTLS, one Brazil.
  Columbia holds a hub contract and the CTLS contract. Vitalant holds a hub contract and the Brazil
  contract.
- **Base period versus project period.** The Brazil record's title says "base period" September 30,
  2026 to September 29, 2027, yet RePORTER lists a project period to 2033-09-29 for it and for the
  DCC. The records don't explain the difference, and we don't assume options, renewals or terms.
  The one fact all seven share is the start, 2026-09-30. For the four hubs and the CTLS, the listed
  period is the base year.
- **The abstracts say "phase 3."** The hub, DCC and CTLS abstracts say each contract "is for phase
  3," which they define as dissemination of findings, closure of databases, and "provision of all
  deliverables to NHLBI." That has a direct IT meaning: this round is heavy on finishing, publishing
  and closing out the databases. Whether a contributing center sends *new* recurring extracts in
  this period is something your hub must tell you in writing. The scenario's invitation says
  recurring extracts, so RSH-0107 starts with that question.
- **The contract numbers start with 75N980.** They are NHLBI contracts. Don't over-read anything
  else about the numbers.

The abstract's own phase definitions also give you the sequence: Phase 1 (years 1–2) for protocols
and a pilot linked database; Phase 2 (years 3–5) for compiling the database and analysis; Phase 3
(years 6–7) for dissemination, database closure and deliverables. The paper's own April 2019 to
March 2026 dates predate the September 2026 round. The records and the paper are two honest
sources describing different slices of time, and neither is wrong.

### Contracts versus grants, in general terms

You'll hear "grant" and "contract" used loosely. In general terms, NIH uses a **grant** to support
research a recipient proposes, with the recipient shaping the work. It uses a **contract** to buy
defined deliverables for the government's own purposes, so NIH directs more of the work. REDS is
funded through contracts, which is why the RePORTER records read as "deliverables to NHLBI." This
matters to you in one way: the program's requirements travel down to participants through the
agreements below the prime contracts. A general starting point for how federal research-and-
development contracts work is FAR Part 35, linked in Resources. **This lesson does not describe any
REDS contract's clauses, because we have not seen any and will not invent them.** What you must get
from the hub is the actual document that binds Lakeshore.

NIH's Data Management and Sharing policy states in its Section III that it applies to research
funded or conducted by NIH "by extramural grants, contracts, Intramural Research Projects, or other
funding agreements." That scope sentence is why a contract-funded program can't treat data sharing
as optional. Module 4 covers what follows.

## What a contributing blood center commits to

At a high level, IT commitments cluster into five areas. Each previews a module:

| Commitment | What it means at Lakeshore | Where taught |
|---|---|---|
| **Recurring extracts** | A scheduled job (EXT-21) reads BECS and produces the donor, donation and component data the program defines | Module 2 |
| **Secure transfer** | Delivery to the program's receiving environment over an agreed secure channel; the paper names sFTP with keys | Modules 2 and 5 |
| **Quality control** | Checks on completeness and format; the paper says submissions are tracked with QC results on dashboards | Module 2 |
| **Change notification** | Telling the hub before a BECS change alters what EXT-21 sends | Modules 2 and 6 |
| **Data protection** | Privacy and confidentiality approvals, a written data agreement, security terms | Modules 3, 4 and 5 |

Two more points keep this honest. First, the paper reports that "a waiver of informed consent was
requested and granted by the single IRB for both hospital patients and blood donors." (An IRB is an
institutional review board, the committee that reviews human-subjects research.) That is the
program's pathway for its own study. It does not decide Lakeshore's privacy obligations. Lakeshore's
privacy officer has to confirm how Lakeshore itself fits, which is module 3. The human-subjects
rules exist in the Common Rule at 45 CFR Part 46, and the local excerpt in `sources/cfr/` is where
that detail will come from.

Second, **the paper says source data are retained "allowing for potential new analyses or
investigations without the need for additional data extractions."** That means what leaves Lakeshore
may live a long time and be reused. A one-line extract request is really a long-lived data
commitment. Module 4 is about that.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it is | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| Josephson et al., *Transfusion* 2022;62(5):982–999 | "Josephson and colleagues, Transfusion, 2022" | Peer-reviewed description of a research program. Not regulation, guidance or standard | Source for the lineage, governance bodies and V2V architecture |
| NIH RePORTER contract records (75N98026D00095 to 00101) | "RePORTER award records for the 2026 REDS contracts" | Federal award records: who holds what contract, for what period | Source for the seven contracts |
| NIH Data Management and Sharing Policy (NOT-OD-21-013), Section III | "the NIH DMS policy, scope section" | NIH funding policy | Says the policy covers research funded through contracts |
| 45 CFR Part 46 (Common Rule) | "forty-five CFR part forty-six" | Regulation on human-subjects protection | Named here only to show the rules exist. Detail is module 3 |

Note what's absent: no CFR row says "REDS." There is no regulation, FDA guidance or AABB Standard
that *requires* a blood center to join REDS. Participation is voluntary and arranged by agreement.
Your regulatory obligations to FDA concern the BECS records, which participation must leave
untouched.

## See it in one picture

The diagram shows the relationships as the records and the paper give them. Solid arrows are
funding and the invitation; the dotted arrows are guidance and a boundary.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    N["NHLBI (with NICHD): funds the program through contracts"]
    N --> H["Regional hub contract holders<br/>(four, per the 2026 records)"]
    N --> D["Data Coordinating Center<br/>(one contract)"]
    N --> C["Center for Transfusion Laboratory Studies<br/>(one contract)"]
    N --> B["REDS Brazil<br/>(one contract)"]
    G["Guide and monitor, per the 2022 paper:<br/>Executive Committee, Steering Committees,<br/>Monitoring Board, External Review Panel"] -.-> H
    H -->|"invitation to contribute"| L["Lakeshore: RSH-0107"]
    L -->|"EXT-21: read-only extract, later modules"| D
    L -.->|"no change to"| R[("BECS records and workflows")]
```

Notice that Lakeshore sits *below* the hub and *beside* its own BECS. The arrow to the DCC is the
paper's architecture; how the hub mediates it is an agreement detail we haven't seen.

## Watch it explained

There's no embeddable video on REDS governance. The closest primary source is NIH's own recording
of the [NHLBI and OASH State of the Science in Transfusion Medicine Symposium 2022 (Day 2)](https://videocast.nih.gov/watch=46109)
on NIH VideoCast: NHLBI's transfusion-research community discussing priorities in the field REDS
works in. It's a long symposium, not a REDS explainer, and it isn't on YouTube, so it's linked rather
than embedded; skim the agenda for the sessions that interest you. The resources page also lists a
podcast transcript with the paper's own authors.

## What an assessor or auditor would look for

For research participation, the "inspector" is as likely to be a hub's site visit, an IRB, your
privacy officer or an internal audit as it is FDA. What each would want to see:

- **A research participation file (RSH-0107)** with the invitation, the signed agreement, the
  approval decisions and a named owner. Bad answer: "It's in someone's email."
- **A written statement of scope**: which fields, which cadence, which destination. Bad answer: "We
  send whatever they asked for last time."
- **Evidence BECS is unaffected.** A read-only design (module 2), and a change-control entry
  linking any BECS change to the extract. FDA's interest is the regulated records, covered in the
  earlier BECS lessons. Bad answer: "The extract user has write access, but it never writes."
- **Evidence of the privacy pathway.** The privacy officer's written confirmation, not a verbal
  "legal said it's fine."

## Common traps

1. **"REDS is NIH, so NIH's rules are our rules."** REDS is a research program funded through
   contracts. What binds Lakeshore is its own agreement, plus rules on the data (module 3 to 5) and
   FDA's rules on the BECS records. Whether any NIH contract term flows down to Lakeshore is a
   question for the agreement, which we haven't seen.
2. **"It's research, so FDA doesn't matter."** The extract is research. The records it reads from
   are not. Regulatory affairs' question has two answers: the program's findings are not FDA
   requirements, *and* the BECS records stay FDA-regulated records. A research job that edits,
   flags or deletes them is a regulated-records problem.
3. **"The new round means a new REDS-V with new rules."** The records show REDS-IV-P phase 3. Ask
   for the current protocol and agreement. Don't assume a successor's requirements, and don't
   promise any.
4. **"Governance bodies are the hub's problem."** They explain why you can't unilaterally change
   an extract's content, timing or use. Treat the hub agreement as the change-control boundary.

## What this means for your job

- **Get the paper trail before the project plan.** Ask the hub for the agreement that would bind
  Lakeshore, the study protocol(s) it covers, and which contract funds them. Don't scope EXT-21
  without them.
- **Answer the CIO in dollars and hours only after scope exists.** Until then, the honest answer is
  "recurring extract, secure transfer, QC, change notification and data protection, sized in
  module 2." Don't guess.
- **Give regulatory affairs a precise answer.** The program is not an FDA requirement. The BECS
  records remain regulated. Participation must not change them.
- **Give the Quality Analyst a design rule.** The extract reads; it never writes, flags or
  reorders BECS data. Any BECS change that affects extract fields goes through change control with
  the extract named.
- **Name one accountable owner per party.** Medical director for the science, privacy officer for
  the legal pathway, you for the service. No orphaned recurring jobs.
- **Escalate when scope grows.** New data elements, new recipients, longer retention or genomic
  data each go back to the privacy officer and the Director before IT builds anything.

## The Director's decision for RSH-0107

You record this, in the file, as a **conditional decision**:

> **Participation in the REDS contribution is approved in principle, subject to the following
> conditions. It is not yet approved to begin transfers.**
>
> 1. The privacy officer confirms the privacy and IRB pathway in writing (module 3).
> 2. EXT-21 is designed as a read-only extract (module 2).
> 3. A written data agreement and security terms are in place (modules 4 and 5).
> 4. No change is made to any BECS record or workflow.

Why conditional? Enthusiasm from the medical director is the reason to say yes. The hub, the
agreement and the privacy pathway are what you haven't seen yet. A yes-in-principle keeps the
relationship moving and keeps IT from building before the paper exists.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: A colleague says "REDS V launched in September, so the rules changed." What do you say?

The records don't support the name. The contracts that started 2026-09-30 are described in RePORTER
as REDS-IV-P "phase 3." A new contract round is real; a formally named REDS-V is not in the records
we hold. Ask the hub for the actual agreement and protocol, and don't assume new requirements.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Is REDS participation an FDA requirement for a blood center? Is it "regulation"?

No. REDS is a research program, and its findings are research evidence, a tier that informs policy
but binds no one. Participation is voluntary and arranged by agreement. This is a "this is not a
regulatory requirement" answer. FDA rules still govern the BECS records the extract reads from.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: The Quality Analyst asks whether research extracts touch BECS records. What's the right design stance, and why?

The extract should read from BECS and never write to it. The records stay regulated (the earlier
BECS lessons cover why), and a research job that alters them creates a data-integrity problem for a
study nobody at FDA asked for. The Director's condition: no change to any BECS record or workflow.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q4: The paper lists an Executive Committee, Steering Committees, a Monitoring Board and an External Review Panel. A board member asks what the Monitoring Board can do. How do you answer honestly?

The paper names it as one of the bodies that "guide or monitor" the program, and the name suggests
independent oversight of the observational studies. But the excerpts we hold don't describe its
charter or powers, so say that and ask the hub rather than guessing.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q5: Explain to your CIO in two sentences what we're signing up for.

"We'd send a recurring, read-only data extract from BECS to a federally funded research program
through a hub, which means secure transfer, quality checks, change notification and data-protection
approvals. The size of the IT cost is set in the next step, once we have the written agreement
and scope, and nothing in our regulated records changes."
:::
